MAFIS

Multi-Agent Fault Injection Simulator

A Resilience Observatory for Lifelong Multi-Agent Path Finding

Teddy Truong · Yannick Francillette
UQAC, Canada · PAAMS 2026

20 s. MAFIS stands for Multi-Agent Fault Injection Simulator. The paper presents it as a resilience observatory for lifelong multi-agent path finding: it tests how robot fleets cope when things go wrong. Everything moving behind me is a real MAFIS run: 40 robots and one planner.

1 million

robots in Amazon warehouses

Source: Amazon, July 2025, reported by TechCrunch

40 s. Amazon announced its one millionth warehouse robot in July 2025. Let me show you what they do all day.
Pick up.Deliver.Repeat.

The robot loads a container from a rack.

It carries it to a station on the right.

Then the next task. Tasks never stop.

1 min. Follow one robot. It loads a container from a rack. Click: it carries it to a delivery station and hands it over. Click: zoom out, every robot does the same, forever. That is lifelong pickup and delivery.

One planner moves them all

Time moves in ticks. Each tick, the planner gives every robot its next move.

Blue dots: where each robot goes next. No two robots may collide.

PIBT

decides one move at a time

RHCR

plans a few moves ahead

Token Passing

robots take turns booking a route

1 min. Software decides every move. We call it the planner. Time moves in ticks, and each tick the planner gives each robot one move, with no collisions. Click: the blue dots show where each robot goes next. We test three planners that work in different ways. PIBT decides one move at a time. RHCR plans a few moves ahead and plans again. With Token Passing, robots take turns booking a route.

League of Robot Runners: the yearly planner competition, run since 2023 with Amazon Robotics

45 s. How does research compare planners? With one number: how many tasks get delivered in a fixed time. Click: and the test assumes every robot moves exactly as planned. That is how the League of Robot Runners, the main competition, scored its earlier editions.

2026

The competition adds delays.

A robot can now be late for a planned move.

League of Robot Runners · 2026 call for participation

Being fast on paper is no longer enough.

1 min. This year the field moved. The 2026 League of Robot Runners, with AAMAS and Amazon Robotics, adds delays: a robot can fail to make a planned move on time. Their words: explicit execution uncertainty through delay probabilities. It even has a track only about handling delays. Click: being fast on paper is no longer enough.

More than delays

BurstWear Zone outageIntermittent

Many robots fail at once, for good.

Robots fail one by one as they age.

One area freezes for a while, as when it loses signal.

Robots pause at random, then resume.

One robot stops. What does it cost the fleet?

1.5 min. Delays are one kind of fault. MAFIS tests four. Burst: 20% of the robots fail at once, for good. Click: wear: robots fail as they age, more often the older they get. Click: zone outage: one strip of the warehouse freezes for 50 ticks, as when it loses its network or power. Click: intermittent: robots pause at random and resume, like the competition’s delays. MAFIS also runs a check, one robot one tick late, the smallest possible fault. You will see it next. Click: so when one robot stops, what does it cost the whole fleet? Nobody had measured it for each planner. That is why I built MAFIS. First: why can a small fault cost so much?

1 / 4 · how small becomes big

Butterfly effect

Two copies of the same run. They move exactly alike.

In one copy, one robot is one tick late.

The change spreads. Red: a robot no longer where its copy is.

One robot, one tick late. ticks later, all 40 robots are somewhere else.

0 / 40 robots no longer where their copy is

Edward Lorenz, 1961: rounding one starting number in a weather simulation changed the whole forecast

1 min. Two copies of the same run, with the same robots and tasks. They move exactly alike, so you see one fleet. Click: in one copy, one robot is one tick late. Click: the change spreads. A robot turns red, with a short ping, the moment it is no longer where its copy is. The bar counts them up to 40. Click: about 250 ticks after one robot was one tick late, every robot is somewhere else. A tiny cause, a different warehouse. Lorenz found the same in a weather simulation in 1961: he rounded one starting number and got a different forecast. (If asked: the work done still matches, 169 vs 168 tasks. So MAFIS judges a fault by the work lost, not by robot positions, and uses this one-tick delay as its smallest possible fault.)

2 / 4

Waiting chains

Robots queue at a station and hand over their containers.

The robot at the station breaks down.

Each robot waits for the one ahead.

One failure blocks the whole line.

How MAFIS finds these chains: Hönig et al., 2019

1 min. Robots queue at a station and hand over containers. Click: the one at the station breaks down. Click: each robot behind it waits for the one ahead. That is a waiting chain. Click: one failure blocks the whole line.

3 / 4

Phantom traffic jam

22 robots on a loop. Nothing blocks the road.

One brakes for a moment. A jam forms, stays, and moves backward.

Sugiyama et al., 2008: the same test with 22 real cars · The robots follow the driver model of Bando et al., 1995

1 min. 22 robots on a loop, as in Sugiyama’s experiment with real cars. No bottleneck. Click: one brakes for a moment. In a few seconds a jam forms, stays, and travels backward while every robot drives forward.

4 / 4

Cascading failure

Each point of a network carries a load (the fill) up to a limit (the ring).

One point fails. Its load moves to its neighbours.

Pushed past their limit, they fail in turn.

The model: Motter & Lai, 2002 · Real case: the 2003 blackout in the USA and Canada, about 50 million people without power

1 min. Think of a power grid. Each point carries a load, shown by its fill, and can take 60% more before it breaks, shown by the ring. Click: one point fails and its load moves to its neighbours. Click: pushed past their limit, they fail in turn, wave after wave. The 2003 north-east blackout grew this way.

And the opposite

Braess’s paradox

Every driver takes the shortcut: the shortest path.

Shortest is not fastest. It jams.

Close the shortcut. Drivers spread over both routes.

Every trip gets faster.

Braess, 1968 · Seen for real: a highway removed in Seoul (2003), 42nd Street closed in New York (1990)

1 min. The middle road is a shortcut, the shortest path. Every driver takes it, so everyone crowds onto the same roads and they jam. Shortest is not fastest. Click: close the shortcut. Drivers spread over both routes, the jam clears, and every trip gets faster. (If asked, the textbook numbers: 4,000 drivers, long roads always 45 minutes, short roads one minute per 100 drivers. With the shortcut every trip takes 80 minutes, without it 65.) Removing a road made everyone faster. Seoul and New York saw it for real. In warehouses, the same idea is why some aisles are one-way. Intuition fails in both directions, so we measure.

How MAFIS works

Run it twice. Break one on purpose. Compare.

  1. 01Measure

    Run the fleet. Count tasks delivered.

  2. 02Copy

    A twin: same map, robots and tasks.

  3. 03Break

    A fault hits the copy only: 8 robots fail.

  4. 04Compare

    The gap is the fault’s cost: 0 tasks

Chaos engineering: Netflix shuts down its own servers to find weak spots (Netflix Tech Blog, 2011) · steps from principlesofchaos.org

1.5 min. So, how does MAFIS work? Run it twice, break one on purpose, compare. The idea is chaos engineering: Netflix shuts down its own servers on purpose, to find weak spots before real failures do. Step one: run the fleet and count the tasks it delivers. Click: copy the run. Same map, same robots, same tasks, so the twin moves exactly alike. Click: break the copy only. At tick 100, 8 of its robots fail. Click: compare. Nothing else differs, so the gap between the two lines is the fault’s cost. For simulation people: pairing runs on shared random numbers is the method of common random numbers.

1 / 4 · what MAFIS measures

Fault tolerance

What share of the work still gets done?

Tasks after the fault

Twin ·
With fault ·

of the twin’s work still done.

1 min. Of the work the twin did after the fault, what share did the faulty run still do? Click: tasks after the fault, for each run. Click: here the faulty run still did 78% of the twin’s work. It is the overall cost of the fault.

2 / 4

Critical time

How long does the fleet work at less than half its twin’s pace?

of the time after the fault.
Long slumps miss deadlines.

1 min. The line is the pace of the faulty run compared with its twin, averaged over 20 ticks. Click: the line at half pace. Click: every tick below it is shaded, 7.6% of the time here. Two runs can lose the same number of tasks, but deadlines are missed in the long slumps.

3 / 4

Time-weighted gap

Does the gap close, or keep growing?

average gap, with late ticks counting more.
A gap that lasts costs more than one that closes.

1 min. The line is the gap in tasks between the faulty run and its twin since the fault, as a share. Click: each tick counts more the later it comes after the fault. Click: the weighted average, 19% here. A fleet that recovers scores low. A gap that keeps growing scores high.

4 / 4

Cascade spread

How many robots does one fault block?

The failed robots, plus the chain waiting on them at that moment.

45 s. The waiting chain from before, as a number. The failed robots, plus every robot waiting on them, directly or through a chain, at the moment of the fault. It shows how far one fault travels.

One run each: an example, not a ranking

1 min. First use: compare planners when things go wrong. Same fault for all three, eight robots breaking down, and each planner against its own twin. Click: the share of its twin’s work each one keeps. Click: this is one run each, an example. The study repeats it on many random setups.

A good planner is fast and resilient

Today, planners are ranked on speed alone: left to right.

Our three planners, one run each.

MAFIS adds resilience: bottom to top.

1 min. Second use: a new way to judge a planner. Today planners are ranked left to right, by tasks delivered with no fault. Click: our three planners, one run each. Click: MAFIS adds the vertical axis, the share of work kept under faults. A good planner sits top right. Next: why that second axis matters.

The ranking flips

Same map, same robots, same tasks. No fault: PIBT delivers more.

With intermittent faults, RHCR delivers more.

Across random setups, the order flips in . One tick of delay alone does not flip it.

Averages over random setups: PIBT is tasks ahead with no fault and behind with faults (give or take and )

1 min. Why the second axis matters. This is the flip we searched for. Same small warehouse, same tasks, 40 robots. PIBT on the left, RHCR on the right. No fault: PIBT delivers more, and the winner lights up. Click: the same runs with intermittent faults, robots pausing at random. Now RHCR delivers more. Click: we repeated it on 30 random setups. PIBT leads by about 48 tasks with no fault and trails by about 47 with faults. The order flips in 24 of the 30. One robot one tick late leaves PIBT ahead, so the faults cause the flip, not chance. A fault-free test would have picked the wrong planner for this warehouse.

Beyond warehouses

Any system that moves, carries or supplies.

Many already have a digital twin: a simulation of the real system.

Try the fault on the twin first.

1 min. The method is not about warehouses. Rail, power grids, drones, hospitals, road traffic, supply chains. Click: many keep digital twins already. Click: run the twin as it is and with a fault, read the gap, before the real failure comes. These are directions, not results.
